title: Why Did Northern Rock Collapse? £4.45bn Withdrawn in 3 Days
summary:
Northern Rock collapse explained from court and regulator records: the 2007 bank run that opened Britain's 2008 financial crisis.
Savers withdrew £4.45bn in three days. Using the Treasury Committee's 'The run on the Rock', the Bank of England's statements, the FSA's own internal audit and enforcement notices, the National Audit Office's reports and the shareholder rulings up to Strasbourg, we show why a bank that was solvent on paper ran out of cash, which executives the regulator found failed to correct, or repeated, understated bad-loan figures, why shareholders were paid nothing, and what the rescue finally cost.

scenes.say: In three days in September 2007, savers pulled four point four five billion pounds out of a single British bank.

visual.label: withdrawn from Northern Rock in three days

scenes.say: That was nearly a fifth of everything its retail customers had deposited. And it happened on television, with queues outside the branches.

visual.label: of Northern Rock's retail deposits, gone

scenes.say: MPs later called it the first run on the retail deposits of a United Kingdom bank since Victorian times.

visual.text: the first run on the retail deposits of a United Kingdom bank since Victorian Times
visual.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.say: So why did Northern Rock collapse? Not, the courts would say, because it had run out of assets. Because it had run out of cash.
Today we go through the paperwork: the Bank of England's statements, a Commons committee report, the regulator's own internal audit, and a string of court judgments.

visual.title: The paperwork
items: Bank of England / Treasury / FSA statements
Treasury Committee: The run on the Rock
Court of Appeal, Upper Tribunal and Strasbourg rulings

scenes.say: And later, the strangest number in the whole file: why a bank the stock market still valued at hundreds of millions of pounds was judged to be worth exactly nothing.

visual.label: the compensation shareholders were awarded
visual.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.say: Chapter 1. The bank that borrowed the world.

visual.text: The bank that borrowed the world

scenes.chapter: The bank that borrowed the world

scenes.say: Northern Rock was a former building society from the north-east of England. By the summer of 2007 it was the country's fifth-largest bank by mortgage assets.
In June 1998 its total assets were seventeen point four billion pounds. By June 2007 they were one hundred and thirteen point five billion.
That is an average of about twenty-three per cent a year, compounded over nine years.

visual.label: average annual growth in total assets, 1998–2007

scenes.say: Here's the problem. Over the same period, money from ordinary savers grew only from ten point four billion pounds to twenty-four billion.
By the summer of 2007, retail deposits made up just twenty-three per cent of what the bank owed.

visual.label: of liabilities came from retail deposits

scenes.say: The economist Hyun Song Shin set out, from the bank's own accounts, that in June 2007 Northern Rock had forty-five point seven billion pounds of securitised notes, another twenty-six point seven billion of other wholesale funding, and eight point one billion of covered bonds.
The securitised notes came through a vehicle called Granite. Northern Rock bundled mortgages together, and investors bought bonds backed by the repayments.

visual.title: Granite
lines: Mortgages pooled and sold to investors as bonds

scenes.say: Reuters later reported that the strategy relied on wholesale markets for three-quarters of the bank's funding.

visual.label: of funding from wholesale markets, as Reuters reported

scenes.say: The model worked as long as one thing stayed true: that investors would always be there to lend again when old funding came due.

visual.sub: Investors will always be there to roll the funding over.

scenes.say: Chapter 2. The summer the market shut.
On the twenty-seventh of June 2007, Northern Rock warned that its profits would fall short, because its funding costs had risen.
Then, in August, the markets it depended on seized up. Shin dates the bank's demise to the ninth of August, when short-term funding and interbank lending all but froze.

visual.sub: Short-term funding and interbank lending freeze

scenes.say: According to facts agreed before the European Court of Human Rights, Northern Rock alerted its regulator, the Financial Services Authority, on the thirteenth of August.
By the third of September, the three authorities, the Treasury, the Bank of England and the FSA, had agreed in principle to provide emergency support.
In the week of the tenth of September, Northern Rock approached the Bank of England for support.
The official statement came on Friday the fourteenth. The Chancellor had authorised the Bank to lend against appropriate collateral and at an interest rate premium.

visual.title: Liquidity support facility
lines: !Against appropriate collateral and at an interest rate premium

scenes.say: And the statement tried to reassure. The FSA judged that Northern Rock is solvent, exceeds its regulatory capital requirement and has a good quality loan book.

visual.text: The FSA judges that Northern Rock is solvent, exceeds its regulatory capital requirement and has a good quality loan book.

scenes.say: It also named the weak spot plainly: the mortgage securitisation market, on which Northern Rock is particularly reliant.

visual.text: the mortgage securitisation market, on which Northern Rock is particularly reliant

scenes.say: But the news had already leaked. On the thirteenth, the BBC broadcast news of the bank's liquidity problems, before the official announcement.
Chapter 3. The queues.
What followed was a scene Britain had not seen in living memory. Customers queued outside branches to take their money out.

visual.sub: Savers line up outside the branches

scenes.say: Part of the reason was the deposit protection of the time. It covered the first two thousand pounds in full, but only ninety per cent of the next thirty-three thousand.
So a saver with thirty thousand pounds stood to lose up to two thousand eight hundred pounds if the bank failed. Rushing to the branch was not irrational.

visual.label: maximum loss on £30,000 under the old rules

scenes.say: Over three days, depositors withdrew four point four five billion pounds. A Yale study puts the outflow at at least four point six billion.

visual.src: ECtHR, Grainger v UK, 10 Jul 2012; Yale Program on Financial Stability

scenes.src: ECtHR, Grainger v UK, 10 Jul 2012; Yale Program on Financial Stability

scenes.say: The shares collapsed too. On the fourteenth, the Associated Press reported, they fell by thirty-one per cent to four hundred and thirty-eight pence.
Shin argued it was not quite the classic run of the textbooks. In his account, the true run was in the wholesale markets, as maturing loans were not renewed. The queues were the visible part.

visual.text: The true run was in the money markets
visual.sub: The queues were the visible part

scenes.say: On Monday the seventeenth, the Chancellor announced that the government would guarantee all existing deposits. The queues subsided.
The guarantee was widened to new retail deposits on the ninth of October, and to a broader range of liabilities in December.
And from the first of October, the national scheme itself changed. Deposits were now protected in full up to thirty-five thousand pounds.
Chapter 4. The taxpayer steps in.
The emergency loan did not stay small. By the ninth of October the first facility was nearly used up, and a second, secured on all the company's assets, was added.

visual.text: A second facility, secured on everything

scenes.say: By the end of 2007, the Court of Appeal recorded, the Bank of England had lent almost twenty-seven billion pounds, with Treasury guarantees of about twenty-nine billion more.

visual.title: Exposure at 31 Dec 2007
visual.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.say: The government spent the winter looking for a buyer. On the seventeenth of February 2008, the Treasury announced that the private bids did not offer value for money.

visual.title: Northern Rock
lines: Private proposals rejected on value for money
!Bank to be taken into temporary public ownership

scenes.say: Northern Rock would be taken into temporary public ownership, with Ron Sandler as executive chairman.
Parliament passed an emergency law, the Banking Special Provisions Act, dated the twenty-first of February. The next day the shares were transferred to the Treasury Solicitor.

visual.src: Banking (Special Provisions) Act 2008; Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.src: Banking (Special Provisions) Act 2008; Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.say: On that day, a tribunal later recorded, Northern Rock owed the Bank of England twenty-five point two eight billion pounds, almost a quarter of its book assets.

visual.label: owed to the Bank of England on 22 Feb 2008
visual.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.say: The Court of Appeal summed up the paradox in two sentences. It was solvent in balance sheet terms. But it was unable to meet its debts as and when they fell due.

visual.text: It was solvent in balance sheet terms. But it was unable to meet its debts as and when they fell due.
visual.by: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HM Treasury, 2009
visual.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.say: The National Audit Office reviewed the decision in 2009. It found nationalisation was the best option for the taxpayer, but said the Treasury could have assessed the risks more systematically.

visual.title: The nationalisation of Northern Rock
lines: A more systematic assessment of risks was possible

scenes.say: The NAO also noted that, while on state support, the bank kept offering mortgages of up to one hundred and twenty-five per cent of a property's value.

visual.label: loan-to-value on mortgages still offered while on state support

scenes.say: Chapter 5. Who was watching?.
So where was the regulator? In March 2008, the Financial Services Authority published the findings of its own internal audit.
It found four failings in the period leading up to the crisis. One was inadequate specific resource directly supervising the firm.

visual.text: inadequate specific resource directly supervising the firm

scenes.say: Reporting on the audit, the finance magazine The CFO set out the detail. There were no formal records of key meetings with the bank.

visual.title: What the internal audit found
items: No formal records of key meetings
Supervision 'at the extreme end of the spectrum'
visual.src: The CFO, 21 Apr 2008; FSA release, 26 Mar 2008

scenes.say: And between January 2005 and August 2007, three different heads of department were responsible for supervising Northern Rock.

visual.label: heads of department responsible, Jan 2005 – Aug 2007

scenes.say: Compared with the other firms it reviewed, the audit put Northern Rock's supervision at the extreme end of the spectrum on these failings. The FSA's chief executive, Hector Sants, said it was not carried out to a standard that is acceptable, though he added that whether that would have changed the outcome was impossible to judge.

visual.text: not carried out to a standard that is acceptable
visual.by: Hector Sants, FSA chief executive, Mar 2008

scenes.say: MPs went further. The Treasury Committee concluded that the FSA systematically failed in its regulatory duty.

visual.text: the Financial Services Authority systematically failed in its regulatory duty
visual.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.say: But the Committee placed the first blame on the bank itself. It said the directors were the principal authors of the difficulties.

visual.text: the directors of Northern Rock were the principal authors of the difficulties that the company faced since August 2007
visual.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.say: And it described their strategy as a reckless business model, excessively reliant on wholesale funding.

visual.text: the directors had pursued a reckless business model which was excessively reliant on wholesale funding
visual.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.src: Treasury Committee, The run on the Rock, 2008

scenes.say: Then, in 2010, the regulator found something else. Not about funding, but about bad loans.

According to the FSA's final notice, the deputy chief executive, David Baker, knew from December 2006 that one thousand nine hundred and seventeen loans were missing from the bank's impaired-loan figures.

visual.label: loans left out of the impaired-loan figures
visual.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.say: Counting them would have lifted reported arrears from zero point four two per cent to zero point six eight per cent, and possessions from six hundred and sixty-two to two thousand five hundred and seventy-nine.

visual.title: What was reported vs what it should have been
visual.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.say: The FSA found that Mr Baker's conduct demonstrated a lack of integrity. He was fined five hundred and four thousand pounds and banned from the industry.

visual.text: Mr Baker's conduct demonstrated a lack of integrity
visual.by: FSA Final Notice, David Baker, Apr 2010
visual.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.say: The managing credit director, Richard Barclay, was fined one hundred and forty thousand pounds and barred from senior roles, for failures of skill, care and diligence rather than integrity. The finance director, David Jones, was fined three hundred and twenty thousand pounds and banned; the FSA found he too lacked integrity.

visual.title: FSA sanctions, 2010
visual.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010; FSA Final Notice, D. Jones, Jul 2010; FSA Final Notice, R. Barclay, Apr 2010

scenes.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010; FSA Final Notice, D. Jones, Jul 2010; FSA Final Notice, R. Barclay, Apr 2010

scenes.say: All three settled with the FSA, and their fines include settlement discounts. These were regulatory findings, set out in final notices. They were not criminal convictions.

visual.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.src: FSA Final Notice, D. Baker, Apr 2010

scenes.say: Chapter 6. Worth nothing.

Now, the strangest number in the file. Immediately before nationalisation, Northern Rock's shares stood at ninety pence. The market valued the bank at about three hundred and seventy-nine million pounds.

Shareholders expected compensation. But the emergency law set the rules for valuing their shares. The valuer had to assume that all state support had been withdrawn, and that the bank was in administration.

visual.title: Compensation rules
lines: !Assume all state support has been withdrawn
visual.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.say: Shareholders, including hedge funds, challenged the law. The largest shareholder, SRM, held more than forty-eight million shares. In July 2009 the Court of Appeal dismissed the challenge.

visual.text: Court of Appeal dismisses the challenge
visual.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.src: Court of Appeal, SRM Global v HMT, 2009

scenes.say: The independent valuer, Andrew Caldwell, was appointed in September 2008. In March 2010, he assessed the compensation at nil.

visual.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.say: More than four hundred and forty former shareholders appealed. In October 2011 the Upper Tribunal dismissed every application.

visual.text: Northern Rock's shares had a nil value on 22 February 2008, so that no compensation was due.
visual.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011

scenes.say: In 2012, the European Court of Human Rights declared the shareholders' case inadmissible. It said the government's approach was far from being manifestly without reasonable foundation.

visual.text: far from being 'manifestly without reasonable foundation'

scenes.say: One last appeal reached the Court of Appeal in 2013. It failed by two judges to one, with Lord Justice Lewison dissenting.

visual.src: Court of Appeal, Harbinger v Caldwell, 2013

scenes.src: Court of Appeal, Harbinger v Caldwell, 2013

scenes.say: On the valuer's assumptions, the court noted, the bank's surplus became a deficit of about two point four billion pounds. On those assumptions the valuer found, and the tribunal upheld, that the shares were worth nothing.

visual.label: the balance sheet on the valuer's assumptions
visual.src: Court of Appeal, Harbinger v Caldwell, 2013

scenes.src: Court of Appeal, Harbinger v Caldwell, 2013

scenes.say: Chapter 7. Our analysis.
So what was the final bill? We can now answer it from the audit reports. In 2008 alone, Northern Rock lost one point four billion pounds.
In 2010 it was split in two. A good bank kept the deposits and some mortgages. The rest stayed in public hands to be run down.
In November 2011, Virgin Money agreed to buy the good bank for seven hundred and forty-seven million pounds in cash, potentially rising above one billion.

visual.label: Virgin Money's cash price for Northern Rock plc

scenes.say: The National Audit Office put the taxpayer's loss on that part at four hundred and eighty million pounds, against an investment of one point four billion.

visual.text: The taxpayer is expected to lose a total of £480 million on the original investment of £1.4 billion in Northern Rock plc.

scenes.say: Across the whole rescue, the NAO counted thirty-seven billion pounds of cash support. UK Financial Investments, which managed the state's stake, expected that cash to be repaid, but the NAO said there could be a net present cost of around two billion pounds.

In May 2016, a Cerberus-led consortium completed its purchase of thirteen point three billion pounds of former Northern Rock mortgages. The NAO found the price was seventy-four million pounds above face value.

visual.label: former Northern Rock mortgages sold, completed May 2016

scenes.say: Here is our reading of the record. Northern Rock did not fail because its borrowers stopped paying. It failed because it borrowed short to lend long, on a scale its savers could never cover.
The regulator, by its own audit, was not watching closely enough. And inside the bank, the FSA later found, the arrears figures had been flattered.

visual.title: Three failures on the record
items: A funding model built on markets that could close
A regulator that, by its own audit, under-supervised
Arrears figures that the FSA found were understated

scenes.say: The shareholder cases are the part most explainers skip. The courts accepted a simple idea: value created by a taxpayer rescue does not belong to the people who owned the bank before it.

visual.sub: The courts: not the old shareholders

scenes.say: Whether that was fair is still argued. One Court of Appeal judge disagreed. But the shareholders lost in every court and tribunal that heard them.

visual.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011; Court of Appeal, Harbinger v Caldwell, 2013; ECtHR, Grainger v UK, 10 Jul 2012

scenes.src: Upper Tribunal, NR Applicants v Caldwell, 2011; Court of Appeal, Harbinger v Caldwell, 2013; ECtHR, Grainger v UK, 10 Jul 2012

scenes.say: And the queues did change the rules. Full protection of deposits, rather than ninety per cent, dates from that autumn.

visual.label: deposit protection up to the limit, from Oct 2007

scenes.say: Northern Rock was solvent on paper and broke in practice. That gap is where bank runs live.

visual.text: Solvent on paper. Broke in practice.

scenes.say: Every source for this episode is numbered in the description. If we've got something wrong, tell us, and we'll correct it.
The next case file is Patisserie Valerie, the cafe chain whose accounts did not add up. Subscribe so it's waiting for you.

shorts.title: Who paid for Northern Rock? The final bill #Shorts
shorts.blurb: The taxpayer's bill for Northern Rock, from National Audit Office reports.

scenes.say: Taxpayers lost four hundred and eighty million pounds on the part of Northern Rock sold to Virgin Money, according to the National Audit Office.

visual.label: taxpayer loss on Northern Rock plc

scenes.caption: £480m loss

scenes.say: The state had put one point four billion pounds of capital into the new bank. Virgin Money paid seven hundred and forty-seven million in cash at the sale, with more possible later.

visual.src: NAO, HC 20, May 2012; HM Treasury, 17 Nov 2011

scenes.caption: £747m cash at sale

scenes.say: Across the whole rescue, the NAO counted thirty-seven billion pounds of cash support, which the state's investment arm expected to be repaid.
scenes.caption: £37bn of support

scenes.say: But the NAO said there could be a net present cost of around two billion pounds. The full story is on our channel.
scenes.caption: Possible cost: ~£2bn
